idea: At each position you decide one thing: is the best sum ending here my running sum plus this number, or is it better to start fresh from this number? A negative running sum is never worth keeping.
analogy: Walking a road that goes up and down, tracking your best climb: if your total since the last restart has gone below zero, you'd do better to start counting again from here.

computeWithKadane.summary: Keep the best sum ending at the current index and the best seen overall.
steps: Start both currentSum and maxSum at nums[0] (handles all-negative arrays).
For each next number: currentSum = max(num, currentSum + num). Start fresh or extend.

computeWithDP.summary: dp[i] = best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at i.
steps: The answer is the largest dp[i]. This is Kadane before squeezing dp into one variable.
computeWithDP.spaceWhy: The dp array of n values.

computeWithDivideConquer.summary: The best subarray is in the left half, in the right half, or crosses the middle.
steps: Split at mid and solve each half recursively.
maxCrossingSubarray finds the best sum that must include mid and mid + 1: extend left from mid, extend right from mid + 1, add them.
Return the largest of the three.
computeWithDivideConquer.timeWhy: log n levels of splitting, each doing O(n) crossing work.
computeWithDivideConquer.spaceWhy: The recursion depth is log n.

computeWithBruteForce.summary: Try every start i and extend the end j, keeping a running sum.
steps: For each start, add elements one by one.
computeWithBruteForce.timeWhy: n starts × up to n ends.

pitfalls: Starting maxSum at 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array; the answer must be the largest single number.
Mixing up "best ending here" and "best overall"; you need both.
interview: Explain the start-fresh-or-extend decision; that's Kadane in one sentence.
Follow-up: return the start and end indices → remember where currentSum last restarted.
The divide-and-conquer version is a common follow-up to test recursion.
